title: Long Tasks, Memory & Leaks
objectives: Explain the allocate-use-release lifecycle and what the garbage collector can and cannot free
Recognize the three most common JavaScript leak patterns in real code
Run the three-heap-snapshot comparison workflow to localize a leak
Use WeakMap and WeakRef so caches never outlive their keys
body:
Memory performance is the art of not keeping dead objects alive. The garbage collector frees anything unreachable, so a leak is never an object the code forgot — it is an object your code still references: a timer holding a closure, an array that only grows, a DOM node detached from the document but parked in a JavaScript variable.

## The problem
Your SPA runs fine for ten minutes, then scrolling stutters and the tab hits 800 MB. A restart fixes it. You need to find *which* objects accumulate — the GC will not tell you, because technically nothing is garbage.

## Constraints
- GC is invisible when healthy: pauses are short and memory falls back to a stable baseline after a feature is used and closed.
- A `setInterval` keeps its entire closure — captured DOM nodes, arrays, listeners — alive until cleared.
- Event listeners on `document` or long-lived stores outlive the component that added them unless explicitly removed.
- Unbounded caches (a Map keyed by user id, an array of every loaded row) are slow leaks disguised as features.

## Options
Fix the classic three:

```js
// 1. Timers: always pair set with clear on teardown
const id = setInterval(poll, 1000)
onUnmounted(() => clearInterval(id))

// 2. Detached nodes: null the reference after removing the element
this.panel.remove()
this.panel = null                  // otherwise GC must keep the whole subtree

// 3. Unbounded caches: bound them (LRU) or tie lifetime to keys
const cache = new WeakMap()        // entry dies when its key object dies
cache.set(widget, computedFor(widget))
```

`WeakMap` and `WeakRef` let you attach data to an object without keeping that object alive — the right default for caches keyed by objects you do not own. `FinalizationRegistry` exists for exotic cleanup but is nondeterministic; do not build features on it.

## Tradeoffs
Weak-keyed caches can be evicted at any GC, so they suit memoization, not persistence. An LRU with a byte budget is predictable but needs eviction code and tests. The three-snapshot workflow costs minutes per investigation — cheap compared to shipping a leak that every long-session user pays for.

## Decision
Default to explicit teardown for every timer, listener and subscription (framework lifecycle hooks make this cheap). Choose WeakMap for memoization keyed by objects, an LRU for value caches with a hard cap. When memory still climbs, stop guessing and take heap snapshots.

## Measure it
The heap snapshot workflow: (1) snapshot at baseline, (2) repeat the suspicious interaction three times, (3) snapshot again, (4) compare — sort by retained size delta and look for growing constructor names and *Detached* DOM trees. Cross-check with the Memory chart in the Performance panel: sawtooth that trends upward is the signature of a leak; a flat sawtooth is healthy.

## Best practices
- Clear every timer and remove every listener in the owning component teardown.
- Keep caches bounded: LRU, max-size, or WeakMap keyed by objects you do not own.
- Null out references to removed DOM subtrees held in long-lived code.
- Compare three heap snapshots over a repeated interaction, not two.
- Watch the memory sawtooth after each fix and confirm it returns to baseline.

## Common mistakes
- Storing DOM elements in module-level arrays and never pruning, then wondering why detached trees pile up.
- Assuming a `WeakRef` cache is a persistence layer — entries vanish whenever GC runs.
- Profiling memory on a 30-second session where no leak has had time to appear.
- Fixing symptoms with `window.location.reload()` instead of finding the retaining reference.
- Reading the Memory chart only, without snapshots — the chart shows *that* it leaks, snapshots show *what* leaks.

exercise.prompt: Build a leak-risk classifier. Each pattern in the list describes a code situation; classify each as leak risk or safe, with a one-line reason (timer not cleared, listener not removed, unbounded cache, WeakMap, cleared timer, bounded LRU). The classifier currently marks everything safe — fix it.
hints: Group the three risky kinds first, then treat everything else as safe.
Return the reason with the verdict: e.g. leak risk — timer keeps its closure alive.
WeakMap and bounded LRU are the two cache patterns that are genuinely safe.

questions.prompt: Why does an uncleared setInterval cause a memory leak?
options: Timers run on the GPU and leak video memory
The timer holds its closure alive, so everything it captures stays reachable
Each tick allocates a new thread that is never joined
The garbage collector pauses while any timer is scheduled
questions.explanation: As long as the interval is scheduled, its callback and everything captured in the closure remain reachable — reachable objects are, by definition, not garbage.

questions.prompt: In the heap snapshot workflow, why take three snapshots of the interaction instead of two?
options: Three is the minimum the Memory panel allows
To separate one-time warmup allocations from memory that grows on every repetition
Because snapshots are averaged by the browser
To capture GPU memory, which snapshots skip otherwise
questions.explanation: The first interaction often allocates one-time caches; only repeated interactions reveal the objects that accumulate every single time.
